## The question

What proportion of tagged fish was detected at each monitoring station? This example uses `tidyr::complete()` to include combinations that have no recorded row, so the calculation includes all tagged fish in its denominator.

```{r setup}
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
```

## The data

The built-in `tidyr::fish_encounters` dataset records detections of tagged fish moving downstream. Each recorded row identifies a fish and a station, with `seen = 1`. There are no explicit rows for nondetections.

```{r data}
fish_encounters |> head(10)

n_fish <- n_distinct(fish_encounters$fish)
n_stations <- nlevels(fish_encounters$station)
n_possible <- n_fish * n_stations

tibble(
  fish = n_fish,
  stations = n_stations,
  possible_combinations = n_possible,
  recorded_rows = nrow(fish_encounters),
  missing_combinations = n_possible - nrow(fish_encounters)
)
```

There are **`r n_fish` fish** and **`r n_stations` stations**, giving **`r n_possible` possible combinations**. Only **`r nrow(fish_encounters)`** are recorded. The other **`r n_possible - nrow(fish_encounters)`** combinations are implicit missing values: the rows do not exist.

## Why the original average is misleading

```{r recorded-only}
recorded_summary <- fish_encounters |>
  summarise(share_detected = mean(seen), .by = station)

recorded_summary
```

Every average equals 1 because every recorded row is a detection. This answers a question about recorded encounters, rather than the proportion of all tagged fish detected at a station.

## Make the missing combinations explicit

```{r complete-grid}
fish_full <- fish_encounters |>
  complete(fish, station, fill = list(seen = 0), explicit = FALSE)

fish_full |> head(15)
```

`complete(fish, station)` creates every combination of fish and station. `fill = list(seen = 0)` marks the new combinations as nondetections. `explicit = FALSE` limits filling to newly created rows, preserving any existing `NA` values.

Here, zero means **no detection was recorded**. It does not prove that a fish was absent, died, or never passed the station. Interpreting a missing row as a nondetection is appropriate for this encounter dataset; in other datasets, a missing row could mean a measurement was never taken.

```{r check-grid}
stopifnot(
  anyDuplicated(fish_full[c("fish", "station")]) == 0L,
  nrow(fish_full) == n_possible,
  sum(fish_full$seen == 1) == nrow(fish_encounters),
  sum(fish_full$seen == 0) == n_possible - nrow(fish_encounters)
)

tibble(
  original_detections = sum(fish_full$seen == 1),
  added_nondetections = sum(fish_full$seen == 0),
  total_combinations = nrow(fish_full)
)
```

## Calculate the proportion using all tagged fish

```{r station-summary}
station_summary <- fish_full |>
  summarise(
    fish_detected = sum(seen),
    fish_in_cohort = n(),
    share_detected = mean(seen),
    .by = station
  ) |>
  arrange(station)

station_summary |> knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

Each station now has the same denominator: all **`r n_fish` tagged fish**. The resulting proportions describe detections within this cohort, rather than the reliability of the monitoring equipment or fish survival.

```{r detection-plot, fig.width=9, fig.height=5}
ggplot(station_summary, aes(station, share_detected, group = 1)) +
  geom_line(color = "#1F4E79") +
  geom_point(color = "#1F4E79", size = 2.5) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(
    title = "Share of tagged fish detected at each station",
    subtitle = "Stations ordered from upstream to downstream",
    x = "Monitoring station", y = "Proportion of tagged fish detected"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 35, hjust = 1))
```

`station` is a factor whose levels follow river order. `complete()` uses all factor levels, and the plot retains this order.

## A nondetection followed by a later detection

The complete grid also lets us identify fish missed at a station but detected farther downstream.

```{r later-detection}
missed_then_seen <- fish_full |>
  mutate(position = as.integer(station)) |>
  mutate(furthest_detection = max(position[seen == 1]), .by = fish) |>
  filter(seen == 0, position < furthest_detection) |>
  select(fish, station)

missed_then_seen
```

This returns **`r nrow(missed_then_seen)` fish-station combination(s)**. A downstream detection supports the interpretation that the earlier nondetection does not establish that the fish stopped migrating. It does not identify the reason for the missed detection.

## Why `explicit = FALSE` matters

Suppose an existing row has an unknown measurement. We may want to keep that unknown value while filling only combinations that were absent entirely.

```{r existing-missing-values}
example <- tibble(
  fish = c("A", "A", "B"),
  station = c("upstream", "downstream", "upstream"),
  seen = c(1, NA, 1)
)

example |>
  complete(fish, station, fill = list(seen = 0), explicit = FALSE)
```

The existing unknown value for fish A stays `NA`. The newly added downstream row for fish B becomes zero. Without `explicit = FALSE`, the default behavior would replace the existing `NA` with zero as well.

## Takeaways

- Check whether missing information is a blank cell or an absent row.
- Use `complete()` to build the combinations relevant to your question.
- Fill with zero only when zero has a defensible meaning.
- Use `explicit = FALSE` when existing unknown measurements should remain unknown.
